title: KV cache compression and quantization
summary: Why the KV cache caps batch size and context, and how to shrink it: share heads (GQA, MLA, CLA), use fewer bits (KIVI, FP8), keep fewer tokens (H2O, SnapKV) or read fewer (Quest, DuoAttention).
outcomes: Compute KV cache bytes per token and per batch from a real model config such as Llama 3 8B
Explain how MQA, GQA, MLA, cross-layer sharing and low-rank projection shrink the cache, and which need training
Explain why keys are quantized per channel and values per token, and compute the cost of scales and the residual
Explain how pre-RoPE keys, outlier handling and FP8 scales keep quantization error low
Compare windows, sinks, H2O, SnapKV and PyramidKV, including how they fit fused kernels and GQA
Explain how Quest's page bounds and DuoAttention's retrieval heads avoid irreversible eviction
Measure key outliers, quantization error and needle accuracy under compression on a real model

lessons.title: Sizing the KV cache of Llama 3 8B, and why it caps batch size

blocks.md: From the prerequisite course you know the **KV cache**: during decoding, every layer keeps the key and value vectors of every earlier token so they are not recomputed. Its size is fixed by the model's shape, the number of tokens, and the bytes used per number.

blocks.tex: \text{bytes per token} = 2 \times n_{\text{layers}} \times n_{\text{kv heads}} \times d_{\text{head}} \times \text{bytes per value}
blocks.caption: The 2 counts one key and one value vector per KV head per layer.

blocks.md: Plug in a real model. The Hugging Face `config.json` of **Llama 3 8B** lists `num_hidden_layers: 32`, `num_attention_heads: 32`, `num_key_value_heads: 8` and `hidden_size: 4096`, so each head has $d_{\text{head}} = 4096 / 32 = 128$. The Llama 3 paper's Table 3 gives the same shape. In **BF16** (bfloat16, the 16-bit *brain floating point* format from Google Brain: 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits and 7 mantissa bits, so the range of a 32-bit float with less precision), each number takes 2 bytes:

blocks.prompt: Llama 3 8B's config has max_position_embeddings 8192, the longest context it was built for. Serve a batch of 32 sequences, each 8192 tokens long. Is the KV cache bigger or smaller than the roughly 16 GB of BF16 weights?
blocks.reveal: **About twice as big.** One 8192-token sequence needs $128 \text{ KiB} \times 8192 = 1$ GiB (1.07 GB). Times 32 sequences that is 32 GiB, or **34.4 GB**, against **16.1 GB** of weights (8.03 billion parameters, counted from the same config, at 2 bytes each). The weights are shared by every request; the cache is per request, so it is what grows with batch and context.

blocks.title: KV cache of Llama 3 8B vs context length

scenes.caption: Llama 3 8B as shipped: 8 KV heads, BF16, batch 8. The cache grows linearly with context and crosses the 63.9 GB left on an 80 GB GPU after weights near 61K tokens per sequence.
Counterfactual: the same model with one KV head per query head (32, plain multi-head attention). Every point is 4x higher; batch 8 runs out of memory near 15K tokens.
Back to 8 KV heads, but store the cache in FP8, an 8-bit floating-point format (1 byte, lesson 4). The line halves, so twice the tokens or twice the batch fit.

2-bit codes plus one FP16 scale and zero point (the two numbers that map codes back to values, lesson 3) per 32 numbers: 2 + 32/32 = 3 bits, or 0.375 bytes. Simplified: real systems also need activation memory and allocator slack.

blocks.md: The formula hands you the levers. You can shrink $n_{\text{kv heads}}$ (share keys and values across query heads, lesson 2), shrink bytes per value (**quantization**, lessons 3 and 4), or shrink the number of tokens kept or read (**eviction** and **selection**, lessons 5 to 7). Lesson 8 tries quantization and eviction on a real model. The first lever is decided when the model is trained; the other two can be applied at serving time.

Memory is only half the story. In the prerequisite course you saw that each decode step must read the whole cache from HBM. A cache that is 4x smaller is also 4x fewer bytes to stream per step, so compression can raise speed as well as capacity, if the kernels read the compressed form directly.
KV bytes scale with layers x KV heads x head size x bytes per value x tokens x batch. Weights are paid once; the cache is paid per token per request, so at long context and large batch it dominates.
A common slip is to use `num_attention_heads` (32) instead of `num_key_value_heads` (8) for a GQA model like Llama 3. That overstates its cache by 4x.

blocks.question: A model has 40 layers, 8 KV heads, head size 128, and stores its cache in FP8. How many bytes per token?
options: 163,840 bytes
81,920 bytes
655,360 bytes
40,960 bytes
blocks.explain: $2 \times 40 \times 8 \times 128 \times 1 = 81{,}920$ bytes. 163,840 forgets that FP8 is 1 byte, 655,360 uses 32 heads at 2 bytes, and 40,960 drops the factor of 2 for keys plus values.

blocks.question: You double the batch size and halve the context length per request. What happens to the total KV cache?
options: It doubles
It halves
It stays the same
It grows 4x
blocks.explain: Total cache is proportional to batch x tokens per sequence. $2 \times 0.5 = 1$, so the cache is unchanged, though per-step attention work per sequence drops.

lessons.title: Sharing keys and values across heads: MQA and GQA

blocks.md: In standard **multi-head attention (MHA)** each of the $H$ query heads has its own key head and value head, so the cache stores $H$ key and $H$ value vectors per layer per token. Shazeer's 2019 paper *Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need* observed that incremental decoding (generating one token per step, each step reading the cached keys and values of all earlier tokens) is slow because of the memory bandwidth spent repeatedly loading these large key and value tensors.

**Multi-query attention (MQA)** keeps all $H$ query heads but shares a **single** key head and value head across them. The cache shrinks by a factor of $H$. The paper reports much faster decoding with only minor quality degradation.

**Grouped-query attention (GQA)**, from Ainslie et al. (2023), interpolates. Query heads are split into $G$ groups and each group shares one key and value head. GQA-$G$ names the version with $G$ groups, so $G$ KV heads per layer: GQA-1 is MQA and GQA-$H$ is MHA. Llama 3 uses GQA with 8 KV heads; its paper says this was done to improve inference speed and reduce KV cache size during decoding.

blocks.title: 8 query heads sharing KV heads (toy, one layer)

scenes.caption: GQA with 4 groups: each pair of query heads reads one shared KV head. The cache holds 4 key and 4 value vectors per token in this layer instead of 8.
MQA (GQA-1): all 8 query heads read the same KV head. The cache is 8x smaller than MHA, but every head must now attend using identical keys and values.

Llama 3 8B mapped onto this picture: read each circle as 2 of its 32 query heads and each cylinder as 1 of its 8 KV heads (half a layer shown). Each KV head serves 4 query heads, so the cache is a quarter of MHA's.

blocks.title: Llama 3 8B shape: KiB per token, then sequences that fit

scenes.caption: Same 32 layers, head size 128 and BF16 for all three; only the KV head count changes. 512, 128 and 16 KiB per token.
Max 8192-token sequences in the 63.9 GB left after weights on an 80 GB GPU (simplified, ignoring activations): 14 for MHA, 59 for GQA-8, and about 476 for MQA.

blocks.md: Why not always use MQA? The GQA paper notes that MQA can degrade quality, and that training a separate model just for faster inference may not be desirable. Its recipe **uptrains** an existing MHA checkpoint: mean-pool the key and value projection matrices (the learned weights that turn each token's hidden vector into its key and value heads) within each group into one head, averaging them entry by entry, then continue pre-training for about 5% of the original compute. Uptrained GQA reached quality close to MHA with speed close to MQA. For their large model the authors chose 8 groups as a middle ground.
GQA and MQA are architecture choices. They need training (or uptraining) and cannot be switched on at serving time, but they stack with every serving-time trick in the rest of this course.
GQA does not reduce attention FLOPs per query head: each query head still scores every cached token. It reduces the bytes stored and read, which is what decode is bound by.

Head count is not the only architectural knob. Three other designs change what is stored per token:

- **Multi-head latent attention (MLA)**, from DeepSeek-V2, caches one compressed **latent** vector per token per layer ($d_c = 512$ numbers) plus one 64-number key shared by all heads that carries RoPE, and rebuilds every head's keys and values from the latent. DeepSeek-V2 (60 layers) stores $(512 + 64) \times 60 = 34{,}560$ numbers per token, which its paper equates to GQA with only 2.25 groups.
- **Cross-Layer Attention (CLA)** (Brandon et al., 2024) lets adjacent layers share one set of keys and values. With a sharing factor of 2 (CLA2) each pair of layers stores one cache, halving it again on top of MQA or GQA. Like GQA, it is trained in: the paper trains 1B and 3B models from scratch.

- **Palu** (Chang et al., 2024) works on a model that is already trained. It factors each key and value projection matrix $W \approx AB$ with a singular value decomposition, caches the short intermediate vector $h = xA$ instead of the full key or value, and rebuilds keys from $h$ on the fly (RoPE prevents folding the key up-projection away; the value up-projection is fused into the output projection). Ranks per layer are chosen from Fisher information (how sharply the loss reacts to changing a weight) measured on 2048 samples of Wikitext-2 (Wikipedia text, lesson 4), with no fine-tuning. The paper reports 50% KV cache compression with strong accuracy, including on Llama-3-8B-Instruct.

All three still fit the lesson 1 formula: CLA halves the layer count that stores a cache, MLA replaces $2 \times n_{\text{kv heads}} \times d_{\text{head}}$ by $d_c + 64$, and Palu replaces it by the kept rank.

scenes.caption: KiB per token in BF16, 32 layers, head size 128: 512, 128, 64, 64, 36 and 16. CLA2 and the MLA row are counterfactual (Llama 3 was not trained with them); the MLA row uses DeepSeek-V2's 512 + 64 numbers per layer.

blocks.question: A team wants to cut KV memory of an already-deployed MHA model by 4x tomorrow, with no training budget. Which is a realistic option?
options: Switch the config to 4x fewer KV heads
Uptrain to GQA with 5% of pre-training compute overnight
Remove 3 of every 4 layers
Quantize the cache from 16 to about 4 bits
blocks.explain: Changing num_key_value_heads without uptraining gives weights that no longer match the architecture. Uptraining costs 5% of the original pre-training run, far from overnight. Quantizing the cache needs no training, which is why the next lessons focus on it.

blocks.question: In GQA with 32 query heads and 8 KV heads, what does each KV head serve?
options: A group of 4 query heads
One query head; the other 24 are unused
All 32 query heads
8 consecutive tokens
blocks.explain: Query heads are split into 8 groups of 4, and each group shares one key head and one value head.

blocks.question: You serve the released Llama 3 8B checkpoint and may not pretrain or uptrain it. Which of these architectural levers can you still apply?
options: Cross-Layer Attention with sharing factor 2
Switching to MLA with a 512-number latent
Palu's low-rank projection of the K and V weights
Dropping to one KV head (MQA)
blocks.explain: Palu decomposes the trained K and V projection matrices with SVD, picks ranks from a small calibration set and needs no fine-tuning. CLA, MLA and MQA change what the attention layer computes, so the model must be trained or uptrained with them.

lessons.title: Quantizing keys per channel and values per token (KIVI)

blocks.md: **Quantization** stores each number as a small integer plus shared scaling information. The simplest scheme is asymmetric **round-to-nearest**: a group of numbers shares a **scale** $s$ and a **zero point** $z$, and each number becomes an integer code $q$ between $0$ and $2^b - 1$ for $b$ bits. *Asymmetric* means the range runs from the group's own minimum to its own maximum instead of being centered on zero; the zero point marks where it starts. Because $s$ and $z$ come from each group's own numbers when it is stored, no **calibration** is needed: the offline pass over sample inputs that some schemes use to pick scales in advance.

blocks.tex: z = \min(X),\quad s = \frac{\max(X) - \min(X)}{2^b - 1},\quad q = \operatorname{round}\!\left(\frac{x - z}{s}\right),\quad \hat{x} = q\,s + z
blocks.caption: Asymmetric b-bit quantization of one group X. Zero point z is the group minimum. b bits give 2^b codes, 0 to 2^b - 1, so the range max minus min is cut into 2^b - 1 equal steps of size s. Each number is stored as its distance above z in steps, rounded; dequantizing gives x-hat = q times s plus z.

blocks.md: Work it on row t0 of the toy key cache below, at 2 bits (codes 0 to 3). Its minimum is $-0.9$ and its maximum $9.1$, so $z = -0.9$ and $s = 10/3 = 3.33$. The value $0.4$ sits $1.3$ above $z$, which is $0.39$ steps, so it rounds to code 0 and comes back as $-0.9$. Rounding to the nearest step can miss by up to half a step, $s/2$, so the wider a group's range, the larger the error of every number in it. The figures score each scheme by **mean squared error** (MSE): the average over all entries of $(x - \hat{x})^2$.

The design question is which numbers share a group. The cache for one head is a matrix with one row per **token** and one column per **channel** (a coordinate of the head vector). **Per-token** quantization groups a row; **per-channel** quantization groups a column. The KIVI paper (Liu et al., 2024) studied KV caches of real models and found that keys have a few fixed **outlier channels** with very large magnitude, while values show no obvious outlier pattern.

blocks.title: Toy key cache: 6 tokens x 6 channels, 2-bit

scenes.caption: Toy keys shaped like the KIVI finding: channel c3 is an outlier channel near 10 for every token; the rest sit in [-1, 1]. Real heads have 128 channels.
Per-token 2-bit: each row shares one range, which c3 stretches to about 10, so the step is 3.2 to 3.9. Almost every small entry collapses to the row minimum. MSE 0.84.
Per-channel 2-bit: each column gets its own range. c3 spans only 8.7 to 11.2 and the small channels keep their own fine steps. MSE 0.026, about 33x lower, at the same 2 bits.
Back to the original keys for comparison. The outlier is confined to its own column, so per-channel groups keep its error out of the other channels.

blocks.md: Why do keys matter so much? A query vector $q$ (here $q$ is the query, not the integer code from before) scores each cached key $k$ with the dot product $q \cdot k$. **Softmax** turns the scores into attention weights: each weight is $e$ to its score divided by the sum of $e$ to every score, so the weights are positive and add up to 1. Scores are first divided by $\sqrt{d}$, with $d$ the number of channels. This is the original Transformer paper's argument: if the channels are independent with mean 0 and variance 1, a dot product of $d$ terms has variance $d$, so dividing by its standard deviation $\sqrt{d}$ keeps scores in a range where softmax does not pile almost all the weight on one token. Take a toy query $q = (1, -1, 0.5, 0.1, -0.5, 1)$ that mostly ignores the outlier channel, as many heads do, and compare softmax weights over the 6 tokens computed from the original and the two quantized key caches (6 channels, so scaled by $1/\sqrt{6}$).

blocks.title: Attention weights of one query over the 6 toy keys

scenes.caption: Exact keys: tokens t0, t2 and t4 get about 0.29, 0.29 and 0.27 of the attention.
Per-token 2-bit keys: small channels were erased, so the pattern is scrambled. t2 jumps to 0.39 and t0 falls to 0.11.
Per-channel 2-bit keys: weights stay within 0.03 of exact (0.29, 0.06, 0.26, 0.05, 0.30, 0.04).

blocks.md: Values are used differently: the attention output is a weighted mix of value **rows**. KIVI argues that per-token quantization confines each value's error to its own token, so a token with low attention weight contributes little error. Their simulated test on Llama-2-13B (fake quantization: the cache is quantized and dequantized again, so only the accuracy effect is measured; group size 32) uses CoQA, a conversational question-answering benchmark where the model answers a chain of related questions about a passage, scored by exact-match accuracy. It makes the asymmetry concrete: 16-bit scored 66.37; 2-bit with keys per-channel and values per-token scored 63.53; 2-bit with both per-token scored 52.93; both per-channel scored 2.88; keys per-token and values per-channel scored 2.80.

You can compute the asymmetry on the toy instead of taking it on trust. Take a 6 x 6 value cache with **no** outlier channel, but with rows of different sizes: tokens t1, t2 and t5 have value entries up to about 2.4, the others stay within 0.4 (real value vectors also differ in size from token to token). The query is the same as before, so the exact attention weights are 0.29, 0.05, 0.29, 0.05, 0.27, 0.05, and the output is the weighted mix $o = \sum_j w_j v_j$. Quantize the values to 2 bits both ways and compare $\|\hat{o} - o\| / \|o\|$, the output error relative to the output's size.

blocks.title: Toy value cache: 6 tokens x 6 channels, 2-bit

scenes.caption: Exact values. Weight 0.29 goes to t0, 0.29 to t2 and 0.27 to t4; t0 and t4 are small rows, t2 a large one.
Per-channel 2-bit: each column's range is set by the large rows (c0 spans -1.9 to 2.1, a step of 1.33), so small t0 and t4 entries move by up to 0.67. MSE 0.107.
Per-token 2-bit: each row gets its own range, so t0 and t4 keep fine steps (0.17 for t0) and only the large, mostly ignored rows get coarse. MSE 0.065.

blocks.title: Attention output error on the toy values (2-bit)

scenes.caption: Relative output error: 0.18 per-token vs 0.57 per-channel, about 3x, at the same 2 bits and group size. Per-channel let the large rows set the step for the heavily weighted small ones.

blocks.prompt: Per-channel grouping needs a group of tokens, but decoding produces one token at a time. How can you quantize a key channel when only 5 new tokens have arrived?
blocks.reveal: You cannot form the group yet. KIVI splits the cache into a **grouped** part, already quantized, and a **residual** part of recent tokens kept in **full precision**. When the residual reaches $R$ tokens (128 in their experiments, a multiple of the group size 32), keys are quantized per-channel as a block and appended. Values use a queue: the oldest full-precision value is popped, quantized per-token, and appended. Attention combines both parts with tiled matrix multiplication: the scores over the quantized block and over the full-precision residual are computed as two products, then joined.

blocks.title: KIVI key cache during decoding (toy residual length R = 4)

scenes.caption: After 3 tokens: all keys sit in the full-precision residual (fp). No group of 4 exists yet.
Token 4 fills the residual. The 4 keys are quantized per-channel to 2 bits as one block (q2) and the residual is emptied.
Tokens 5 to 7 accumulate in a fresh residual. Attention reads 4 quantized keys plus 3 full-precision ones.
At token 8 the second block is quantized. Simplified: KIVI uses R = 128 and groups of 32, so up to 128 recent tokens stay in full precision.

blocks.md: The scales and zero points cost memory too. With one FP16 scale and one FP16 zero point per group of 32 numbers, that is $16 + 16 = 32$ extra bits shared by 32 numbers, or $32 / 32 = 1$ extra bit per number, so 2-bit codes cost about 3 bits each. For Llama 3 8B that is $128 \times 3/16 = 24$ KiB per token instead of 128 (3 bits in place of BF16's 16). The KIVI paper reports 2.6x less peak memory including weights, up to 4x larger batch, and 2.35x to 3.47x throughput on Llama, Falcon and Mistral.

The full-precision residual has a price too. Count the worst case for one 8192-token Llama 3 8B sequence: 128 recent tokens of keys and values in BF16, $128 \times 128$ KiB $= 16$ MiB, plus $8064 \times 24$ KiB $= 189$ MiB of 2-bit codes with scales. That is 205 MiB against 1,024 MiB in BF16, **5.0x** smaller (5.3x if the residual is ignored). For short sequences the residual dominates: at 256 tokens it is $128 \times 24 + 128 \times 128 = 19{,}456$ KiB against 32,768 KiB, only 1.7x smaller. This is the figure lesson 7 uses for capacity.

Keys: quantize per channel, because outliers live in fixed channels. Values: quantize per token, because the output mixes value rows. Keep the most recent tokens in full precision until a group is complete.
Bits per number are not the whole cost. Group metadata adds bits (about 1 per number for FP16 scale and zero per 32), and the full-precision residual matters for short sequences.

blocks.question: A colleague quantizes both keys and values per-token at 2 bits and sees accuracy collapse, while 4-bit per-token worked fine. What is the most likely fix?
options: Use 3-bit per-token for both
Quantize values per-channel and keep keys per-token
Quantize keys per-channel and keep values per-token
Add more calibration data
blocks.explain: Per-token key groups get their range stretched by outlier channels, which wipes out the small channels at 2 bits. Per-channel keys fix that. In KIVI's Llama-2-13B test, keys per-token with values per-channel scored 2.80 on CoQA, worse than all per-token.

blocks.question: In the toy, per-channel 2-bit keys reached MSE 0.026 while per-token 4-bit keys reached 0.028. What does this suggest?
options: Bit width matters more than grouping axis
Choosing the right axis can matter as much as two extra bits
The toy is broken, since 4 bits must always win
Outlier channels only matter for values
blocks.explain: With the right grouping, 2 bits matched what per-token needed 4 bits for, because the range of each group no longer includes the outlier. 4 bits does not win automatically when its groups mix scales.

blocks.question: In the toy, per-channel value quantization had higher MSE and 3x the output error. Which change to the toy would shrink the gap between the two schemes most?
options: Make every value row the same size, so no row stretches another's column range
Use a sharper query so even more weight lands on t0, t2 and t4
Add one outlier channel to the keys
Use 2-bit codes with a smaller group of 3 tokens for keys
blocks.explain: Per-channel hurt because the large rows widened every column range and the small, heavily weighted rows paid for it. If all rows had similar ranges, each column's range would be similar to each row's, and the two schemes would give similar errors. Changing the keys does not touch value quantization.

lessons.title: Beyond rounding: pre-RoPE keys, outliers, and FP8 in production

blocks.md: **KVQuant** (Hooper et al., 2024) pushes below 4 bits with several additions. It keeps per-channel key quantization and adds: quantizing keys **before RoPE** (the position encoding explained next), per-layer **non-uniform** number formats (the $2^b$ levels are not evenly spaced but placed where that layer's values cluster, chosen offline from sample data), keeping a small fraction of **outliers** in a separate sparse full-precision store, and keeping the first token in FP16. The paper reports under 0.1 perplexity degradation at 3 bits on Wikitext-2 and C4 for LLaMA, Llama-2, Llama-3 and Mistral.

**Perplexity** is the standard score for how well a language model predicts held-out text; lower is better. For each true next token the model gave some probability $p$. Average $-\ln p$ over all tokens (that average is the cross-entropy loss) and raise $e$ to it. If the model always gave the true token probability 1/4, the average is $\ln 4$ and the perplexity is 4: as unsure as a fair pick among 4 tokens. So under 0.1 of degradation means the 3-bit cache predicts text almost as well as the 16-bit one. **Wikitext-2** is about 2 million tokens of good and featured Wikipedia articles, and **C4** (Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus, from Google's T5 paper) is cleaned web text.

**RoPE** (rotary position embedding, Su et al.) treats each pair of key channels as a point in a plane and rotates it by the angle position x $\theta$, where each pair has its own fixed rate $\theta$, fast for the first pairs and slow for the last. Queries are rotated the same way. A rotation preserves lengths and angles, so the score of a query at position $m$ with a key at position $n$ depends only on the difference $(m - n)\theta$. That helps attention know relative positions, but it mixes the two channels of a pair by a different amount at every position. A channel that had a steady large value before RoPE swings between large positive, near zero and large negative afterwards.

blocks.title: One channel pair before and after RoPE (toy: 0.5 rad per position)

scenes.caption: Before RoPE, channel a is steady near 8 and b is near 0. Each column has a narrow range, ideal for per-channel groups.
After RoPE, the pair is rotated by 0.5 rad x position. Column a now spans -6.77 to 8.0 and b spans 0.3 to 8.19: the steady outlier became a swinging one.

blocks.title: Per-channel quantization MSE on the toy pair

scenes.caption: Same 12 numbers, same per-channel scheme. Quantizing before rotation gives 0.004 vs 0.93 at 2 bits, and 0.001 vs 0.12 at 3 bits. Rotation preserves length, so pre-RoPE error stays the same after RoPE is applied.

blocks.md: The catch is that the cache then holds un-rotated keys, so RoPE must be applied after dequantization on every read. KVQuant writes a fused kernel to do this on the fly: one GPU kernel that dequantizes the keys, applies RoPE and multiplies them by the query in one pass, without writing full-precision keys back to memory. It reports a 0.82 perplexity improvement on Wikitext-2 for 3-bit LLaMA-7B from pre-RoPE quantization alone.

Two more KVQuant pieces target rare large values. **Dense-and-sparse** quantization pulls the largest-magnitude values of each vector out into a sparse full-precision list, so they no longer stretch the range of the rest; removing 1% of values this way gave a further 0.19 perplexity gain for 3-bit LLaMA-7B. And because of the **attention sink** effect (models put large attention on the first token, lesson 5), the model is disproportionately sensitive to error in that token, so KVQuant keeps the first token in FP16.

**FP8** is an 8-bit floating-point format, with two common variants named by their bit split. **E4M3** has 1 sign bit, 4 exponent bits and 3 mantissa bits, and its largest value is 448; **E5M2** trades a mantissa bit for range, up to 57,344. Because the range is limited, values are divided by a **scale** before the cast and multiplied by it when read back. A **per-tensor** scale is one number for a whole layer's keys (or values); a per-head scale is one number per attention head.

Production engines mostly ship a simpler option: an **FP8** cache. vLLM's `kv_cache_dtype` accepts `"fp8"`, `"fp8_e4m3"` and `"fp8_e5m2"`, and supports a per-tensor scale or, with calibration from llm-compressor (the vLLM project's library for quantizing checkpoints), per-attention-head scales. Without calibration, all scales default to 1.0. TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA's open-source LLM inference library) supports INT8 and FP8 KV caches with a per-tensor `kv_cache_scaling_factor` of shape [1]; values are quantized when written and dequantized on the fly inside the attention kernel.

# BF16 weights, FP8 (e4m3) KV cache: half the bytes per cached token.
llm = LLM(model="meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct",
          kv_cache_dtype="fp8")
# Without calibrated scales, vLLM uses scale 1.0 for K and V.
# For calibrated per-tensor or per-head scales, quantize the
# checkpoint with llm-compressor first (see the vLLM docs).
blocks.caption: Enabling an FP8 KV cache in vLLM, following its quantized KV cache docs.

blocks.title: FP8 KV cache: quantize on write, dequantize on read

nodes.label:
multiply by 1 / scale,
cast to FP8

scenes.caption: Write path: each new token's keys and values are scaled and cast to FP8 once, when they enter the cache.
Read path: every decode step streams the FP8 cache, half the bytes of BF16, and dequantizes inside the attention kernel (TensorRT-LLM's description).

Variation: vLLM notes that with the FlashAttention 3 backend (the third version of the FlashAttention kernel, built for NVIDIA Hopper GPUs) and an FP8 cache, attention itself runs in FP8 and queries are quantized too.

blocks.md: Rounding error depends on the range of each group. Pre-RoPE keys, per-channel groups, sparse outliers and an FP16 first token all exist to keep group ranges narrow.

FP8 without calibration uses a scale of 1.0. That works when values fit FP8's range, but calibrated scales are what vLLM recommends for best accuracy, and some layers (such as sliding-window ones, which attend only to a fixed number of recent tokens) can be kept in the native dtype, the model's own number format.

blocks.question: Why does KVQuant quantize keys before applying RoPE?
options: RoPE rotates channel pairs by position-dependent angles, so a steady outlier channel becomes inconsistent across tokens
RoPE makes keys larger, which overflows FP16
RoPE is only applied to values
Post-RoPE keys cannot be cached at all
blocks.explain: Per-channel quantization relies on each channel having a consistent range across tokens. Position-dependent rotation spreads a large channel's energy into its partner, widening both ranges. The cost is reapplying RoPE after dequantization.

blocks.question: Your FP8 KV cache (no calibration) is accurate on most layers but one sliding-window layer degrades. Which change targets that directly?
options: Switch every layer to 2-bit KIVI
Increase the batch size
Use FP8 e5m2 for weights
Keep that layer's cache in the native dtype and the rest in FP8
blocks.explain: vLLM documents `kv_cache_dtype_skip_layers` (for example `["sliding_window"]`) for exactly this: sensitive layers stay in the model's dtype while the rest use the quantized cache.

lessons.title: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters

blocks.md: Quantization keeps every token but stores each one more cheaply. **Eviction** keeps a fixed **budget** of tokens and drops the rest. The bet is that attention is sparse: the H2O paper (Zhang et al., 2023) reports that attention matrices of LLMs are over 95% sparse at inference time, so most cached tokens get almost no weight.

The obvious policy is a **sliding window**: keep the most recent $W$ tokens. StreamingLLM (Xiao et al., 2023) showed that it fails badly once text exceeds the window. Llama-2-13B on a 65K-token book had perplexity 5158 with a 1024-token window, but 5.40 when the cache kept the first 4 tokens plus the 1020 most recent. A perplexity of 5158 means the model was as unsure as picking among about 5158 tokens: its predictions had collapsed.

The reason is the **attention sink**: models put large attention on the first few tokens even when they are not semantically important, apparently as a place to park attention that softmax forces to sum to 1. Evict them and the attention distribution shifts. StreamingLLM found 1 or 2 initial tokens are not enough and 4 generally suffice.

**H2O** (Heavy-Hitter Oracle) adds content awareness. It sums each cached token's attention scores over the steps so far; tokens with large sums are **heavy hitters**. The cache keeps a balance of heavy hitters and recent tokens, and when full it evicts the non-recent token with the smallest accumulated score. The paper finds keeping only heavy hitters or only recent tokens is worse than both together.

Toy setup for the figure (synthetic logits, the raw attention scores before softmax, computed by script): 12 tokens; token 0 is a sink, tokens 2 and 5 carry key content, and the last two tokens get a recency boost. Budget: 5 cached tokens plus the current one. Rows are the queries of tokens 6 to 11; columns are keys 0 to 11. Values are full-cache attention weights.

blocks.title: Which keys each policy can still see (budget 5 + current)

scenes.caption: Full cache. Most weight lands on token 0 (0.30 to 0.48), token 2 (0.12 to 0.17) and token 5 (0.14 to 0.18, and 0.49 for q6, where it is also recent); the rest is a thin recency diagonal.
Sliding window: only the 6 most recent keys. Token 0 is gone from the first row on, then 2 and 5. On average only 43% of the full attention weight is still visible.
StreamingLLM style: token 0 kept as a sink plus the 4 most recent. The sink alone restores much of the mass (78%), but tokens 2 and 5 still fall out of the window.
H2O: 2 recent slots plus 3 slots for the highest accumulated scores. From q8 on, tokens 0, 2 and 5 hold those slots; visible mass is 93%.

blocks.prompt: In the H2O run, token 3 had an accumulated score of 0.23 and was evicted when token 8 arrived, while token 0 had 4.36. Suppose the user's next question is about the content of token 3. What happens?
blocks.reveal: It is gone for good. Eviction is **irreversible**: H2O decided from past attention, and a token that was unimportant so far can become crucial later. Quantization degrades every token a little; eviction loses some tokens completely. That is why retrieval-style tests (finding one fact in a long document) are the standard stress test for eviction methods.

blocks.md: One more detail makes StreamingLLM work: positions are assigned **within the cache**, not in the original text. With cached tokens [0, 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8] and token 9 being decoded, the positions used are 0 to 7. For RoPE models it caches keys before rotation and applies RoPE at each step, the same pre-RoPE idea as KVQuant for a different reason.

H2O looks free to deploy in the toy, but its score is a running sum of the attention each cached token receives, so every decode step must produce, for every head, the weights of all cached tokens. Fused kernels such as FlashAttention never write the attention matrix to memory: they loop over tiles of keys and keep only running softmax statistics, so those weights do not exist outside the kernel. You need a second scoring pass (more reads of the keys), a modified kernel that also emits per-key sums, or slow unfused (eager) attention. Quest's authors ran H2O at 100K tokens by using FlashAttention for the prompt and collecting H2O scores only during decoding; kvpress's H2O-style `ObservedAttentionPress` requires eager attention. **SnapKV** (lesson 7) instead compresses the prompt once, right after prefill, scoring prompt tokens by the attention they get from the last few prompt queries, its **observation window** (16 to 64 queries). That small window x prompt block is all it needs, so kvpress computes it separately and leaves the main kernels alone.

GQA adds a second mismatch: attention weights exist per **query** head, but the cache is stored per **KV** head and one KV entry serves the whole group. Evicting per query head would need a separate copy of the group's keys and values for each query head. Ada-KV (lesson 6) points out that the original code of SnapKV and PyramidKV (both in lesson 7) did exactly that, replicating the grouped cache across heads; its fix, also used by kvpress, averages the scores of the query heads in a group and keeps or evicts one entry per KV head. For Llama 3 8B that is the difference between 4 copies and 1.

Eviction scores are not free under fused attention. A method that needs every step's attention weights (H2O) needs eager attention, a second pass or a custom kernel. A method that scores once after prefill (SnapKV) leaves the decode kernel unchanged. With GQA, combine the scores over each group before choosing.
Eviction trades exactness for a fixed memory budget. Keep the sink tokens, keep recent tokens, and use accumulated attention to keep the heavy hitters; anything evicted cannot be recovered.

Accumulated sums favor older tokens, which have had more steps to collect attention. In the toy, every later token entered with a tiny sum and was evicted within a few steps of leaving the recent slots.

blocks.question: A chat service uses a pure 4096-token sliding window. After the conversation passes 4096 tokens, output turns to gibberish. What is the most targeted fix?
options: Make the window 8192 tokens
Quantize the window to 4 bits
Also keep the first few tokens as attention sinks
Recompute the whole window every step
blocks.explain: The collapse begins when the initial tokens leave the window, so the softmax loses its sink. Keeping 4 initial tokens restored Llama-2-13B from perplexity 5158 to 5.40 in StreamingLLM. A bigger window only delays the failure.

blocks.question: Which statement about H2O is correct?
options: It needs the model to be fine-tuned
It scores tokens by attention they received in past steps, as a proxy for future importance
It keeps every token but at lower precision
It keeps only heavy hitters and no recent tokens
blocks.explain: H2O is training-free and uses local statistics: the sum of attention each token received so far. The paper finds this as effective as using future attention, and that keeping both heavy hitters and recent tokens is needed.

blocks.question: Your server runs an unmodified FlashAttention kernel for both prefill and decode, and you can afford one small extra computation right after prefill. Which method can you deploy without touching the kernels?
options: H2O, because its scores are a by-product of decoding
Both, since FlashAttention returns attention weights on request
SnapKV, because it scores the prompt once from a small observation window
Neither, since every eviction method needs the full attention matrix
blocks.explain: SnapKV only needs the observation window's attention over the prompt, a window x prompt block you can compute in a separate small pass once, after which the decode kernel reads an ordinary (shorter) cache. H2O needs per-key attention every decode step, which FlashAttention never materializes.

lessons.title: Keep everything, read less: query-aware pages and head-aware budgets

blocks.md: Every token-reduction method so far makes the same bet: decide now which tokens will never matter, and delete the rest. Lesson 5 showed how that bet loses when a later question needs an evicted token. Two families avoid it. **Quest** keeps the whole cache and, at each decode step, reads only the parts this query is likely to need. **DuoAttention** keeps the whole cache only for the attention heads that actually look far back.

Quest (Tang et al., 2024) starts from an observation: which tokens are critical depends on the current query. In their example prompt "A is B. C is D. A is", token "B" gets almost no attention until the final "is", which needs it. Quest manages the cache in **pages** of a few tokens each, like the fixed-size blocks of PagedAttention from the prerequisite course; its kernels use 16 tokens per page. For each page it stores two extra vectors: the channel-wise minimum $m$ and maximum $M$ of the page's keys, updated whenever a token is added.

blocks.tex: U_{\text{page}} = \sum_{i} \max\left(q_i\, m_i,\; q_i\, M_i\right) \;\ge\; q \cdot k \quad \text{for every key } k \text{ in the page}
blocks.caption: Each term q_i k_i is a straight line in k_i, so over the range from m_i to M_i its largest value sits at one end: at M_i if q_i is positive, at m_i if it is negative. Summing the per-channel maxima bounds every token's score in the page.

blocks.md: Work it on 16 tokens in 4 pages of 4, with 4 channels and query $q_1 = (1, 0.5, 0.5, -1)$. Page 2 holds keys whose channel minima are $m = (0, -1, 0, -3)$ and maxima $M = (3, 1, 2, 1)$. Per channel the larger product is $\max(0, 3) = 3$, $\max(-0.5, 0.5) = 0.5$, $\max(0, 1) = 1$ and $\max(3, -1) = 3$, so $U = 7.5$. The four pages get bounds 3, 5, 7.5 and 1.5. With a budget of 2 pages Quest loads pages 2 and 1 and runs exact attention over those 8 tokens. The best token, t8 with score 7.0, is in page 2; scaled by $\sqrt{4}$ and softmaxed, the two pages hold 89% of the full attention weight.

blocks.title: Quest page selection on 16 cached tokens (budget 2 pages)

scenes.caption: 16 cached tokens in 4 pages of 4. Quest keeps all of them and stores, per page, the channel-wise min and max of its keys. Nothing is scored yet.
Query q1 = (1, 0.5, 0.5, -1) reads only the metadata and gets an upper bound per page: 3, 5, 7.5 and 1.5. The top 2 pages, 2 and 1, are loaded.
Exact scores q1 . k inside each page. The best token, t8 (7.0), is in page 2, and no score in a page exceeds its bound. Pages 1 and 2 hold 89% of the attention weight.
Next step, query q2 = (-1, 0.5, 0, 1). Bounds 2.5, 3.5, 1.5, 4: now pages 3 and 1 are loaded. Page 2 is skipped this step but still in memory.
Exact q2 scores: the best tokens, t6 and t12 (2.5 each), are both in loaded pages, which hold 67% of the weight. Eviction would have had to guess this one step earlier.

blocks.question: A colleague scores each page by q . M alone (the query times the page's max key). In the example that gives page 2 a score of 3.5, yet token t8 inside it scores 7.0. What went wrong?
options: Nothing: q . M is always an upper bound
The query's last channel is negative, so the largest product there comes from the minimum key (-3), not the maximum
Page 2 has too many tokens for the bound to hold
The bound only holds after softmax
blocks.explain: For q_4 = -1 the product q_4 k_4 is largest when k_4 is smallest: t8 has k_4 = -3, giving +3, while q_4 M_4 = -1. Using max(q_i m_i, q_i M_i) per channel covers both signs; q . M alone can underestimate a page and skip the token that matters.

blocks.md: Note what Quest saves. Memory is **not** reduced: the whole cache stays (in GPU memory, or offloaded to CPU memory), and the min and max add 2 key-sized vectors per 16-token page, about 6% more. What shrinks is the bytes read per step: the metadata (about $1/S$ of the cache for page size $S$) plus the $K$ selected pages. With 16-token pages, a 64K context and a 4K-token budget that is $1/16 + 4096/65536 = 1/8$ of the cache. The paper reports up to 7.03x faster self-attention and 2.23x lower end-to-end latency (with 4-bit weights), and keeps the first two layers dense because their attention is not sparse.

On a 10K-token passkey test (LongChat-7B), a **needle-in-a-haystack** test that hides one fact, a random passkey, in long filler text and asks for it at the end, Quest found the key 99% of the time with a 64-token budget; H2O, TOVA (another attention-score eviction method) and StreamingLLM stayed at 8% or below even with 512 tokens, because they had evicted the passkey before the question arrived. At 100K tokens Quest reached 96% with a 1024-token budget.

Eviction decides once and forever from past attention. Query-aware selection decides again at every step from the current query, so a token that was unimportant yesterday can still be read today. It saves bandwidth, not capacity.

**DuoAttention** (Xiao et al., 2024) looks at heads instead of tokens. A few **retrieval heads** attend to relevant tokens anywhere in the context; most **streaming heads** attend only to attention sinks and recent tokens. Each KV head gets a gate $\alpha \in [0, 1]$ that mixes full attention with sink-plus-recent attention. With the model frozen, the gates are trained for 2,000 steps on synthetic data (ten 32-word passkeys hidden in long text) to keep the last hidden states close to the full model's on the passkey tokens, plus an L1 penalty (weight 0.05) that pushes gates toward 0. At deployment gates above a threshold mark retrieval heads; the rest keep only sinks and recent tokens (16 and 64 sufficed in the paper's ablation; its needle and LongBench (a benchmark of long-document tasks, lesson 7) runs used 64 and 256).

After training (toy values): heads whose output changes when cut to sinks plus recent tokens keep high gates; the L1 penalty pushes the rest toward 0.

Deployment: gates above the threshold become retrieval heads with a full cache; the rest are streaming heads with a constant cache of 16 sinks and 64 recent tokens. Here half the heads are retrieval heads.

Decoding 8192 tokens: the retrieval half holds 8192 tokens per head, the streaming half holds 80. The layer's cache is about half the size, and the heads identified as retrieval heads have not lost a token.

blocks.md: Capacity for Llama 3 8B, with half its 256 KV heads as retrieval heads (the ratio the paper uses for GQA models on the needle test): per 8192-token sequence the retrieval half needs $0.5 \times 128 \text{ KiB} \times 8192 = 0.5$ GiB and the streaming half a constant $128 \times 80 \times 2 \times 128 \times 2$ bytes $= 5$ MiB. That is 117 sequences in 63.9 GB instead of 59, about 2x (simplified; with the 64 + 256 tokens of the needle runs the streaming half is 20 MiB and 114 fit). The paper's measured reductions are up to 1.67x memory and 1.50x faster decoding for GQA models (2.55x and 2.18x for MHA), and with 8-bit weights and a 4-bit cache it decodes Llama-3-8B with 3.3 million tokens of context on one A100.

Per-head budgets generalize this. **Ada-KV** (Feng et al., 2024) wraps a top-k eviction method such as SnapKV: instead of giving every head the same budget, it takes the top $B$ attention scores across all heads of a layer at once, so heads whose attention is spread out get more slots and sharply focused heads fewer, with a safeguard that mixes in a share of the uniform budget. It is still eviction, so it reduces memory but can still lose a token.

blocks.md: DuoAttention needs a short optimization per model (several hours on an 8-GPU node, per the paper) and its gates are only as good as the synthetic task; Quest needs a kernel that reads selected pages and computes bounds. Neither is a configuration flag.

blocks.question: A user pastes a 20K-token chat log, then asks for an order number mentioned once near the start. The cache uses either H2O, Quest or DuoAttention at similar budgets. Which can still answer, and why?
options: Only H2O, because order numbers collect attention
Quest and DuoAttention: Quest still holds every token and selects by the new query, and DuoAttention keeps full caches in its retrieval heads
Only DuoAttention, because Quest evicts pages it does not load
None: any method under full size loses distant tokens
blocks.explain: H2O may have evicted the order number long before the question, since it got little attention while the chat went on. Quest only skips pages for a step; the question's query can raise that page's bound and load it. DuoAttention's retrieval heads never dropped a token. Quest's pages are not evicted, only not read.

lessons.title: Compressing long prompts (SnapKV, PyramidKV) and choosing a recipe

blocks.md: H2O decides token by token during decoding. For long prompts (documents, code, or retrieval context: passages that a retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, system fetches from a document store and pastes into the prompt) most of the cache is created at once during prefill. **SnapKV** (Li et al., 2024) compresses it right after prefill. It found that each attention head keeps focusing on the same prompt positions during generation, and that this pattern can be read from an **observation window**: the last few tokens of the prompt.

Per head, SnapKV sums the attention that the observation-window queries give to each earlier prompt token (a **vote**), smooths the votes with 1D max pooling (each vote is replaced by the largest vote within kernel-size positions centered on it; with kernel 3, the max of itself and its two neighbors) so neighbors of a peak are kept as a cluster, keeps the top-scoring positions, and appends the window itself. **LongBench** is a benchmark of long-context tasks such as question answering over long documents, summarization and code completion; a **needle-in-a-haystack** test hides one fact (the needle) at some depth in long filler text and asks the model to retrieve it. The paper's LongBench runs use an observation window of 32 and a max-pooling kernel of 7 (16 and 5 in its needle-in-a-haystack and pooling ablation runs); the figure below uses a toy window of 3 and kernel of 3.

blocks.title: SnapKV selection on a 12-token toy prompt
blocks.code:
def snapkv(attn, window, budget, kernel):
    # attn: [prompt_len, prompt_len] for one head
    obs = attn[-window:, :-window]       # window queries vs prefix keys
    vote = obs.sum(axis=0)               # total attention per prefix token
    pooled = max_pool1d(vote, kernel)    # spread peaks to neighbors
    keep = topk(pooled, budget - window) # pick prefix positions
    n = attn.shape[0]
    return sorted(keep) + list(range(n - window, n))

scenes.caption: Prompt of 12 tokens; tokens 9 to 11 form the observation window. Budget 6: the window plus 3 prefix tokens.
Votes sum the attention from the 3 window queries to prefix tokens 0 to 8. Token 5 is the clear peak; token 8 is an isolated spike.
Max pooling with kernel 3 gives 4 and 6 the peak score of their neighbor 5. Without pooling, top-3 would be [4, 5, 8], splitting the cluster.
Top-3 of the pooled votes keeps the whole cluster [4, 5, 6]. Final cache: 6 of 12 tokens. The paper argues clusters preserve details, such as a full phone number.

blocks.md: SnapKV reports a 3.6x increase in generation speed and 8.2x better memory efficiency at 16K-token inputs, and processing up to 380K tokens on one A100-80GB with a negligible drop in a needle-in-a-haystack test.

**PyramidKV** (Cai et al., 2024) observes that attention is spread widely in lower layers and concentrates on a few tokens in higher layers. So instead of the same budget per layer, it gives lower layers more. With a total budget $k^{\text{total}}$ over $m$ layers and a shape hyperparameter $\beta$, the top layer gets $k^{\text{total}}/(\beta m)$, the bottom layer gets $2k^{\text{total}}/m$ minus that, and layers in between follow an arithmetic sequence. Why that bottom value? In an arithmetic sequence the average of all terms equals the average of the first and last, and the average must be $k^{\text{total}}/m$ for the layers to add up to $k^{\text{total}}$, so bottom plus top is $2k^{\text{total}}/m$. A larger $\beta$ shrinks the top layer's share and makes the pyramid steeper. Token selection inside each layer follows SnapKV.

blocks.title: Per-layer KV budget for a toy 8-layer model (average 64)

scenes.caption: Uniform allocation, as in SnapKV or H2O: 64 tokens in every layer, 512 in total.
PyramidKV with beta = 4: top layer 512 / (4 x 8) = 16, bottom 2 x 512 / 8 - 16 = 112, a straight line in between. Still 512 in total.

blocks.md: The paper reports matching full-cache LongBench performance while keeping 12% of the KV cache.
Putting the course together for Llama 3 8B on an 80 GB GPU with 8192-token sequences (63.9 GB left after weights, ignoring activations and allocator overheads):

blocks.title: Llama 3 8B: 8192-token sequences that fit in 63.9 GB

scenes.caption: Simplified capacity model: 4 GiB, 1 GiB, 0.5 GiB, 205 MiB (2-bit with scales and the 128-token residual, lesson 3) and 0.2 GiB per sequence. GQA gives 4x over MHA; FP8 doubles it again; 2-bit with its residual, or keeping 20% of tokens, gives about 5x.

blocks.md: These levers compose: H2O's paper reports that combining its eviction with quantization did better than either alone in its tests. But each has a different failure mode. Quantization adds small noise everywhere, so check sensitive layers and the first token. Eviction loses tokens permanently, so check retrieval over long contexts. GQA is fixed at training time. FP8 is the low-risk, widely supported option in vLLM and TensorRT-LLM (it must be enabled; vLLM's default `kv_cache_dtype` is `"auto"`, the model's dtype); 2-bit and eviction methods need careful evaluation on your own workload.

Choose by failure mode: FP8 for a near-free 2x; per-channel-key, per-token-value low-bit (KIVI, KVQuant) for 4x to 5x if kernels support it; eviction (StreamingLLM, H2O, SnapKV, PyramidKV) when context length is the problem and occasional lost tokens are acceptable; query-aware reads (Quest) or head-aware caches (DuoAttention) when they are not.
Smaller caches only become speed if the attention kernel reads the compressed form directly. Dequantizing to BF16 in a separate pass gives back most of the memory traffic saved.

blocks.question: A RAG service sends 30K-token prompts and generates 200-token answers. Memory is dominated by prompt KV. Which method fits best?
options: SnapKV-style selection after prefill, guided by the end of the prompt
Sliding window over the last 4096 tokens
MQA conversion with no retraining
H2O with only recent tokens
blocks.explain: The cache is created at once by a long prompt, and the question usually sits at the end. SnapKV uses those final prompt tokens to pick what each head will need. A plain window drops most of the documents.

blocks.question: Why does PyramidKV give lower layers a bigger budget?
options: Lower layers have more heads
Higher layers are skipped at inference time
Lower layers use FP8 already
Attention in lower layers is spread over many tokens, while higher layers focus on a few
blocks.explain: Its analysis shows information funneling: broad attention low, concentrated attention high. Uniform budgets waste slots in high layers and starve low ones.

blocks.question: Using the bars, which move gives the larger capacity gain over GQA-8 BF16: FP8, or keeping 20% of tokens in BF16?
options: FP8, about 2x
They are equal
20% kept, about 5x
Neither changes capacity
blocks.explain: FP8 halves bytes per token (59 to 119 sequences). Keeping 20% of tokens cuts per-sequence cache 5x (59 to 297), but with the risk of losing information permanently.

lessons.title: Build and test it: quantize real keys, then evict on a needle test

blocks.md: Time to see real KV tensors. Everything here runs on a laptop CPU in a fresh virtual environment (`pip install torch transformers kvpress`, tested with torch 2.15, transformers 5.2 and kvpress 0.5.5, with `OMP_NUM_THREADS=2`). The model is **SmolLM2-360M-Instruct**, a small model with the Llama architecture: 32 layers, 15 query heads sharing 5 KV heads (GQA with groups of 3), head size 64, RoPE base 100,000. Part 1 pulls one layer's keys and values out of the cache and quantizes them the lesson 3 way. Part 2 runs eviction methods on a needle test.

blocks.code:
import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM
from transformers.models.llama.modeling_llama import apply_rotary_pos_emb
torch.set_num_threads(2)
M = "HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M-Instruct"  # Llama architecture, GQA 15 q / 5 kv heads
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(M)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(M, dtype=torch.float32).eval()
ids = tok(open("paragraph.txt").read(), return_tensors="pt").input_ids[:, :256]
cap = {}  # pre-RoPE q and k, caught at the projection outputs
for L, layer in enumerate(model.model.layers):
    for n in ("q", "k"):
        getattr(layer.self_attn, n + "_proj").register_forward_hook(
            lambda m, i, o, key=(n, L): cap.__setitem__(key, o.detach()))
with torch.no_grad():
    out = model(ids, use_cache=True)
T, hd = ids.shape[1], 64
cos, sin = model.model.rotary_emb(cap["k", 0], torch.arange(T)[None])
def heads(x, n): return x.view(1, T, n, hd).transpose(1, 2)
L = 2
k_pre = heads(cap["k", L], 5)
q_post, k_rot = apply_rotary_pos_emb(heads(cap["q", L], 15), k_pre, cos, sin)
k_post = out.past_key_values.layers[L].keys      # what the HF cache stores
v = out.past_key_values.layers[L].values
print("cache keys are post-RoPE:", torch.allclose(k_post, k_rot, atol=1e-4))
mag = k_pre[0, 0].abs().amax(0)                  # per-channel max |k|, KV head 0
top = mag.argsort(descending=True)[:4].tolist()
print("top channels", top, "max |k|", [round(mag[c].item(), 1) for c in top],
      "median", round(mag.median().item(), 2))
blocks.caption: Part 1a: run 256 tokens of a paragraph, catch pre-RoPE queries and keys at the q_proj and k_proj outputs, and read post-RoPE keys and values from the Hugging Face cache (layer 2).

blocks.md: Two details matter. Hugging Face caches keys **after** RoPE, so to get pre-RoPE keys you hook the key projection (`k_proj`) and rotate them yourself with the model's own `rotary_emb`; the script checks that rotating its hooked keys reproduces the cache exactly. And in this layout RoPE rotates channel $i$ together with channel $i + 32$, not with its neighbor, at a rate of $100000^{-2i/64}$ radians per token: about 1 for pair 0 but only 0.00025 for pair 23.

blocks.code:
def quant(x, bits=2, axis="token", g=32):       # x: [tokens, channels]
    y = x if axis == "token" else x.T
    y = y.reshape(y.shape[0], -1, g)
    lo, hi = y.amin(-1, keepdim=True), y.amax(-1, keepdim=True)
    s = (hi - lo).clamp(min=1e-8) / (2**bits - 1)
    y = (torch.round((y - lo) / s) * s + lo).reshape(x.T.shape if axis != "token" else x.shape)
    return y if axis == "token" else y.T
def rope(k): return apply_rotary_pos_emb(k[None, None], k[None, None], cos, sin)[1][0, 0]
mask = torch.ones(T, T).triu(1).bool()  # causal
def attn(q, k, v):
    w = (q @ k.T / hd**0.5).masked_fill(mask, -1e9).softmax(-1)
    return w @ v
def report(h):
    Kpre, Kpost, V = k_pre[0, h], k_post[0, h], v[0, h]
    Q = q_post[0, 3*h:3*h+3]  # 3 query heads share KV head h
    ref = [attn(q, Kpost, V) for q in Q]
    def err(K, Vv=V):
        return sum(((attn(q, K, Vv) - r).norm(dim=-1) / r.norm(dim=-1))[-64:].mean()
                   for q, r in zip(Q, ref)).item() / 3
    rows = {"keys per-token, post-RoPE": quant(Kpost, axis="token"),
            "keys per-channel, post-RoPE": quant(Kpost, axis="channel"),
            "keys per-channel, pre-RoPE": rope(quant(Kpre, axis="channel"))}
    for name, K in rows.items():
        print(f"{name:28s} MSE {((K - Kpost)**2).mean():.3f}  out err {err(K):.3f}")
    for ax in ("token", "channel"):
        print(f"{'values per-' + ax:28s} MSE {((quant(V, axis=ax) - V)**2).mean():.4f}"
              f"  out err {err(Kpost, quant(V, axis=ax)):.3f}")
report(0)

blocks.md: Read the numbers against the earlier lessons. Per-channel key groups beat per-token ones by 21x in MSE here, and across all 160 KV heads of the model (same paragraph, same function) the mean key MSE was 1.14 per-token against 0.173 per-channel post-RoPE and 0.133 pre-RoPE. Pre-RoPE helped in this layer (0.111 to 0.070) but only by a median of 1.26x per head, up to 3.2x: the big outlier channel sits in a slow-rotating pair, so RoPE hardly widens its range, while the fast pairs do widen (c0's range over the 256 tokens grows from 2.4 to 5.3). How much pre-RoPE quantization buys depends on the model and layer; KVQuant's 0.82 perplexity gain was measured on LLaMA-7B. Values tell the lesson 3 story on a smaller scale: similar MSE either way (0.019 vs 0.017), yet per-token values gave the lower output error (0.335 vs 0.411).

blocks.question: On another model your per-channel 2-bit key MSE is 5x higher on post-RoPE keys than on pre-RoPE keys of the same layer. Which lesson explains the gap, and what is the fix?
options: Lesson 3: switch keys to per-token groups
Lesson 4: RoPE rotates channel pairs by position, widening per-channel ranges; quantize before RoPE and rotate after dequantizing
Lesson 5: keep the first 4 tokens as attention sinks
Lesson 7: use SnapKV to drop the noisy tokens
blocks.explain: Per-channel groups work when each channel has a steady range across tokens. RoPE mixes each pair by a position-dependent angle, so fast-rotating pairs swing widely after rotation. KVQuant caches pre-RoPE keys and reapplies RoPE in a fused kernel on read; per-token keys would be far worse.

blocks.md: Part 2 uses **kvpress**, NVIDIA's library of KV cache compression methods ("presses") for Hugging Face models. A press hooks every attention layer, scores the prompt's cached entries during prefill, and drops the lowest-scoring fraction, its `compression_ratio`. `StreamingLLMPress` keeps 4 sink tokens and the most recent ones; `ObservedAttentionPress` keeps the entries that received the most attention during prefill, averaged over the queries that could see each entry, so old tokens get no head start (the H2O idea; it needs eager attention, as lesson 5 explained); `SnapKVPress` scores from the last `window_size` queries (64 by default), smooths with average pooling (kernel 5) rather than lesson 7's max pooling, and averages over each GQA group. The test is the passkey format Quest used: a 5-digit key hidden at a chosen depth in about 2,000 tokens of repeated filler. kvpress's pipeline compresses the context **before** the question is appended, unless you put the question inside the context yourself.

blocks.code:
import random, re, sys, time, json, torch
from transformers import pipeline
from kvpress import StreamingLLMPress, SnapKVPress, ObservedAttentionPress
torch.set_num_threads(2)
pipe = pipeline("kv-press-text-generation", model="HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M-Instruct",
                dtype=torch.float32, model_kwargs={"attn_implementation": "eager"})
FILL = "The grass is green. The sky is blue. The sun is yellow. Here we go. There and back again. "
def haystack(key, depth, n=80):
    lines = [FILL] * n
    lines.insert(int(depth * n), f"The pass key is {key}. Remember it. {key} is the pass key. ")
    return ("There is important information hidden inside a lot of irrelevant text. "
            "Find it and memorize it. " + "".join(lines))
Q = "What is the pass key? Answer with the number only."
def trial(press, key, depth, aware):
    ctx = haystack(key, depth)
    if aware:   # question is part of the compressed prompt (SnapKV paper setting)
        out = pipe(ctx + "\n" + Q, press=press, max_new_tokens=16)
    else:       # kvpress default: compress the context before the question arrives
        out = pipe(ctx, question=Q, press=press, max_new_tokens=16)
    found = re.findall(r"\d+", out["answer"])   # first number in the answer must be the key
    return bool(found) and found[0] == str(key)

from transformers import DynamicCache
class FP8Cache(DynamicCache):            # emulates vLLM kv_cache_dtype="fp8" with scale 1.0
    def update(self, k, v, layer_idx, cache_kwargs=None):
        f8 = lambda x: x.to(torch.float8_e4m3fn).to(x.dtype)   # round to E4M3, store back
        return super().update(f8(k), f8(v), layer_idx, cache_kwargs)
def trial_fp8(key, depth):
    out = pipe(haystack(key, depth), question=Q, cache=FP8Cache(), max_new_tokens=16)
    found = re.findall(r"\d+", out["answer"])
    return bool(found) and found[0] == str(key)

blocks.md: The depth breakdown of this run (10 trials per depth) explains each bar. StreamingLLM's misses are exactly the needles in the span it deletes, the oldest tokens after the 4 sinks: depth 0.1 at 25% removed, 0.1 and 0.3 at 50%, everything but 0.9 at 75%. The H2O-style press also loses the early needles first (0 of 10 at depth 0.1 even at 25%), because, as lesson 5 warned, it scores from prefill attention that the passkey never earned. SnapKV with no question failed at every depth, even depth 0.9. A diagnostic hook on one trial (depth 0.5, 25% removed) showed it kept 92% of the key's digit entries averaged over all heads, but only 38% in layer 0, and one missing digit is enough for the model to answer "42".

The fix was the window, not the method. With the question inside the prompt, the default 64-query window is mostly filler, whose queries look at earlier copies of the same filler, so the vote for the key stays low (28% at best in this run). Shrinking the window to 16 queries, essentially the 13-token question, made SnapKV near perfect even with 75% of the cache gone; the SnapKV paper's own needle runs use a window of 16. FP8 changed nothing at this scale. On a GPU you would run the same harness against vLLM with `kv_cache_dtype="fp8"` (lesson 4's code; **not run here**, no NVIDIA GPU), and the vLLM docs publish no accuracy table, so that measurement is yours to make.

These numbers are one run: one small model, one synthetic task, a 2K-token prompt and 50 trials per bar, so other keys or filler can move a bar by several points. They show failure modes, not rankings: repeated filler is unusually easy for StreamingLLM and unusually hard for windowed voting. Rerun the harness on your own prompts, lengths and model before choosing a method.

Question-aware compression works when the scoring queries are the question. Question-agnostic compression has to guess, and eviction cannot undo a wrong guess. Measure accuracy by needle depth, not only on average.

StreamingLLM drops old documents by position, and FP8 does not reduce the token count.
